passage: I'm Sarika. Last winter our downstairs neighbour came up to complain about water leaking into his ceiling. Fair enough, at first. Then his voice climbed, he kicked our shoe rack across the landing and grabbed the iron rod we use for the window latch. Hafsa, my flatmate, started explaining about the plumber, calmly, the way we'd explain to anyone. I saw his knuckles white on that rod and something in me went very clear. I said, "We'll talk tomorrow," pulled Hafsa back inside, shut the door and bolted it. Then I called the security guard at the gate and the police helpline. The guard came up within minutes, and two constables arrived soon after and spoke to him on the landing. Hafsa was shaking. "I thought if I just explained properly..." I understood. But nobody reasons with a man holding a rod. After that, we took the leak to the society committee, not to him.

qa.q: What did the neighbour grab from the landing?
qa.a: The iron rod used for the window latch.

qa.q: What does "something in me went very clear" suggest about Sarika at that moment?
qa.a: It suggests Sarika felt afraid but focused, recognising real danger and that safety had to come before any talk.

qa.q: Which steps kept them safe, and what came after?
qa.a: Stepping back inside, bolting the door, calling the guard and the police helpline, and later taking the leak to the society committee instead of facing him again.

qa.q: Why was Hafsa shaking afterwards?
qa.a: Hafsa had been trying to reason with the neighbour and was frightened, only then realising how dangerous the moment had been.

grounding: Shows a person who, when a neighbour's anger turns threatening, stops trying to reason, gets out of reach and calls for help.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage:
Thursday night. Seema's diary.
Found Amma's blue vase in pieces behind the sofa cushion. Asked Joseph. "I don't know, Mummy. Maybe the cat?" We don't have a cat that comes inside. His ears went red and he wouldn't look up from his plate. I wanted to shout. Then I remembered hiding a broken cup under my bed at his age, heart thumping. So I sat on the floor with the pieces and said, "Whoever broke this won't be punished tonight. I just want to know, so nobody steps on glass." Long pause. Then a small voice: "It was me. The football." He cried. I hugged him and we swept up together. Next time I'll say the safe part first.

qa.q: What did Seema find behind the sofa cushion?
qa.a: Amma's blue vase in pieces.

qa.q: What did Seema feel on hearing "Maybe the cat?"
qa.a: Seema felt a flash of anger and wanted to shout, but also recognised Joseph's fear from her own childhood.

qa.q: What will Seema do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: Say the safe part first, that nobody will be punished and she just wants to know, because fear of punishment was what made Joseph lie.

qa.q: What was it like for Joseph once Seema said nobody would be punished tonight?
qa.a: Joseph felt safe enough to admit the football broke it, and his fear came out as tears and relief in the hug.

grounding: Shows a parent noticing a child's lie about a broken vase, seeing the fear behind it, and offering a calm, safe way to tell the truth.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage: Nirmala had twenty minutes before her night shift at the hospital, and the bus would not wait. But Dolma had flipped her phone face down again the moment Nirmala walked in, the third time that week, and a new name kept lighting up: "K". Nirmala's chest tightened. A dozen questions crowded her mouth: Who is K? Show me. Since when? She took a breath and sat on the edge of the bed instead. "I noticed the phone flips. You're allowed private things, Dolma. I'm your mother, not a detective. I won't grab it." Dolma's shoulders stayed up. "But my two rules stand: nobody online asks you to keep secrets from me, and you don't meet anyone you only know from the phone. Deal?" Dolma looked at her a long moment. "K is Karma from basketball camp. We're... talking." She went pink. "Okay," Nirmala said, grabbing her bag. "Tell me about Karma tomorrow, if you want."

qa.q: How long did Nirmala have before her night shift?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when Dolma flipped the phone face down?
qa.a: Nirmala felt anxious, her chest tightening as a dozen worried questions crowded in.

qa.q: Which part of Nirmala's approach balanced privacy and safety?
qa.a: She named what she noticed, promised not to grab the phone, and restated two clear safety rules about secrets and meetings instead of interrogating.

qa.q: How might Dolma have felt when Nirmala promised not to grab the phone?
qa.a: Dolma was guarded at first, but being trusted with privacy and given clear rules made it safe enough to say who K was.

grounding: Shows a parent sensing a teenager's secrecy about her phone and answering the worry with open words and clear safety expectations rather than interrogation.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage:
Monday: Deepak's maths result came back, 23 out of 80. He folded the sheet into his geometry box and told Mummy the papers weren't checked yet. It felt like a door clicking safely shut.
Thursday: a parents' meeting notice for next week. Deepak didn't hand it over. He skipped cricket, sat alone in the library pretending to revise, and snapped at Sangeeta didi when she asked why he was so quiet. At night he lay awake rehearsing what he'd say when they found out.
The next Tuesday: Sangeeta found him on the terrace. "You haven't laughed in a week. What's going on?" Deepak's throat closed. Then he pulled out the folded sheet. She read it, sat beside him and said, "Okay. That's bad, not the end. Let's tell Mummy together before the meeting." For the first time in eight days, Deepak's shoulders dropped.

qa.q: What did Deepak score in maths?
qa.a: 23 out of 80.

qa.q: How was Deepak feeling by Thursday?
qa.a: Deepak felt anxious and isolated, skipping cricket, snapping at his sister and lying awake afraid of being found out.

qa.q: What could Deepak try the next time something goes wrong at school?
qa.a: Tell one trusted person early, like Sangeeta didi, before hiding turns a bad mark into a week of fear and loneliness.

qa.q: What was it like for Sangeeta watching Deepak that week?
qa.a: Sangeeta noticed he had not laughed in a week and was worried, and got snapped at when she asked, until he finally showed her the sheet.

grounding: Shows a teenager hiding a failed maths result out of shame, feeling safe at first but growing more isolated and afraid until he tells his sister.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage: Yusuf's scooter came back to the Jayanagar parking lot with a long scrape down the left side and the mirror twisted. Anjali handed over the keys without meeting his eyes. "It was like that when I took it, na?" Yusuf knew it wasn't; he had washed it on Sunday. He felt the heat rise and an accusation form. He swallowed it. "Anjali, sit for a sec." They sat on the low wall. "I'd honestly rather have it straight than be shielded from it. Whatever happened, I'm not going to blow up. It's a scooter." Anjali picked at her dupatta. A long pause. "I skidded on the gravel near the flyover. I was so embarrassed, and you'd just said how new it was." "Were you hurt?" "Just my palm." She showed it. "Okay. We'll get the mirror fixed Saturday." Anjali laughed shakily. "I'll pay for the mirror. And sorry."

qa.q: When had Yusuf washed the scooter?
qa.a: He had washed it on Sunday.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when Anjali said it was like that before?
qa.a: Yusuf felt angry, the heat rising and an accusation forming, because he knew the scooter had been clean and whole.

qa.q: Which of Yusuf's choices made honesty easier?
qa.a: Swallowing the accusation, sitting down with Anjali, and saying he preferred the truth and would not blow up, which made confessing less costly.

qa.q: Why might Anjali have told the truth after Yusuf spoke?
qa.a: His promise not to blow up lowered the cost of honesty, so admitting her embarrassment felt safer than keeping up the story.

grounding: Shows a person who suspects a lie choosing to say he prefers the truth and will not explode, which makes an honest answer possible.

subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
passage: Counselling note, Thursday, 5 p.m. Aadhya, 25, came in holding a printout: the college portal showing her brother Arnab had not attended a single MBA class since March. He had told her every week that classes were "fine, tiring". When she asked last month, he lied again, then twice more. Today she swung between anger ("He looked me in the eye") and self-doubt ("How did I not see it? Am I stupid?"), then cried quietly about "the brother I thought I had". I told her that people who trust are not stupid; they are trusting. We worked on two boundaries she can keep: she will stop covering for Arnab with their parents, and she will not discuss his fees until he tells them himself. She wrote both in her own words. She plans to talk it through with her cousin Riddhi, whom she trusts, before speaking to Arnab on Sunday. Follow-up booked for next Thursday.

qa.q: Since when had Arnab not attended a single MBA class?
qa.a: Since March.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she asked "Am I stupid?"
qa.a: Aadhya felt self-doubt and shame, wondering how she had missed the lies, alongside anger at being deceived.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor help Aadhya take?
qa.a: Naming two boundaries in her own words, no covering and no talk of fees until he tells their parents, and talking to Riddhi, a cousin she trusts, before facing Arnab.

qa.q: What would change if Aadhya kept covering for Arnab with their parents?
qa.a: The lies would stay easy for Arnab and the weight would stay on Aadhya, so trust would keep wearing down with nothing changing.

grounding: Shows a young woman hurt by her brother's repeated lies, feeling anger, self-doubt and grief, and setting boundaries with a counsellor's help and a trusted cousin's support.

passage: At the Chennai bus stop, Harsha was asking the conductor about the route when Vishal tugged her sleeve. "Amma! Amma! Amma, the bus has a elephant painted—" "One minute, kanna." "But AMMA—" Harsha didn't scold. She put Vishal's small hand on her arm and covered it with hers, still listening to the conductor. Vishal hopped from foot to foot, holding on. The moment the conductor stepped away, Harsha squeezed his hand. "Now. Tell me." "The bus has an ELEPHANT on it!" he said. She looked, and it did.

qa.q: What was painted on the bus?
qa.a: An elephant.

qa.q: Why did Vishal keep saying "Amma" so urgently?
qa.a: Vishal was excited and seemed afraid the elephant thought would slip away if he had to wait.

qa.q: What could other parents borrow from Harsha?
qa.a: A quiet signal like the child's hand on the arm, covered by the parent's hand, then a clear "Now, tell me" when it is the child's turn 🙂

qa.q: What was it like for Harsha when Vishal tugged her sleeve?
qa.a: Harsha needed to hear the conductor, but she stayed patient and found a way to show Vishal he would be heard soon.

grounding: Shows a small child interrupting because an exciting thought feels urgent, and a parent teaching waiting with a hand-on-arm signal instead of silencing him.

passage:
"—and then the coach said—"
"Wait, WAIT, the same coach who—"
"Yes! And she—"
"No way, Chaitanya, you're joking!" Bhavna slapped the canteen table, grinning, talking over the last half of every sentence.
Chaitanya stopped and picked at his samosa.
"You okay?" Bhavna asked.
"You keep finishing my sentences. Wrong, mostly."
Bhavna blinked. "I'm just excited! At my house, if you wait for a gap, you never talk. Ma and my aunts all talk at once. It means we're into it."
"At mine, you wait till someone's done. Otherwise it feels like you don't care what I'm saying."
"Oh." Bhavna pressed her lips together, then laughed. "Okay. Tell me the whole coach thing. I'll sit on my hands."
She actually did. Chaitanya grinned and started again from the beginning.

qa.q: Where were Bhavna and Chaitanya talking?
qa.a: At the canteen table.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling while she talked over Chaitanya?
qa.a: Bhavna was excited and eager; her overlaps were meant as enthusiasm, not rudeness.

qa.q: What small change did Bhavna try, and why did it help?
qa.a: She sat on her hands and let him tell the whole story, which showed she cared about his way of talking too 😊

qa.q: How did Bhavna's interruptions come across to Chaitanya?
qa.a: To Chaitanya they felt as if she did not care what he was saying, because in his home you wait till someone is done.

grounding: Shows a teenager talking over a friend out of excitement, and how overlap feels warm in one home and disrespectful in another.

passage: At the agriculture college in Hassan, the soil-testing group met on the verandah after lab. Hafsa began, "If we sample before the rains, the nitrogen reading—" "Yeah, yeah, basically we test early," Eshaan cut in, and the group moved on. Twice more she started; twice more he finished for her, louder. By the end she was drawing circles in her notebook. At Friday's review, Eshaan presented "his idea" of sampling before the rains. Professor Gowda nodded approvingly. Hafsa's face burned. Walking to the bus stand afterwards, her classmate Latha said, "That was your point. I heard you say it on Monday." Hafsa stopped. "He never lets me finish." "Next time, just say you'd like to finish. I'll back you." At the next meeting, when Eshaan cut in again, Hafsa said evenly, "Let me finish, please." Latha nodded. Eshaan sat back. Hafsa finished.

qa.q: Where did the soil-testing group meet?
qa.a: On the verandah after lab.

qa.q: What does Hafsa drawing circles in her notebook suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt unheard and discouraged, and had given up trying to speak in that meeting.

qa.q: What worked at the next meeting, and why?
qa.a: Hafsa calmly asked to finish, with Latha nodding support, which claimed her turn without a fight.

qa.q: Why might Latha have spoken up on the walk to the bus stand?
qa.a: Latha had heard Hafsa's idea on Monday and felt it was unfair to see it credited to Eshaan, so she wanted to back her.

grounding: Shows a student whose points are cut off and later credited to someone else going quiet, then reclaiming her turn by asking to finish.

passage: At the milk cooperative office near Anand, Wasim had a habit his old mentor once pointed out: he talked the most in every meeting. Now, as the new secretary, he kept a small tally in the margin of his notebook. By half past ten the monthly meeting stood at: Wasim, nine lines. Shalini ben, who ran the evening collection, one. The three older members, two each. Wasim looked at the tally, stopped mid-sentence and turned. "Shalini ben, you're at the counter every evening. What are we missing?" Shalini hesitated, then said the chilling unit had shut off twice last week around seven, when the power dipped, and nobody had written it down. The room went quiet. Nobody else had known. They spent the next half hour on a backup plan. When the meeting ended, the tally read: Wasim, eleven; Shalini ben, seven. He underlined it.

qa.q: How many lines had Wasim spoken by half past ten?
qa.a: Nine lines.

qa.q: Why did Wasim stop mid-sentence after checking his tally?
qa.a: Wasim felt a jolt of awareness, a little uncomfortable, seeing how much of the airtime he had taken as secretary.

qa.q: What habit is Wasim building, and why does it matter in his role?
qa.a: Counting his own turns and inviting quieter members in; as secretary his voice carries weight, so making space brings out problems others see.

qa.q: What was it like for Shalini ben to be asked directly?
qa.a: She hesitated at first, but the direct question gave her room to raise the chilling unit problem nobody else knew about.

grounding: Shows a person who tends to talk a lot counting his own turns and asking a quieter member for input, which brings out a hidden problem.
